Approximation and inapproximability results transfer in both directions without loss.

Regional information bound: for every X⊆V, at least ceil(log2(|X|+1)) bugs must be hosted in N[X]. Moreover, the optimum is additive over connected components.
If every connected component C has a universal safe house, then OPT is exactly sum_C ceil(log2(|C|+1)), computable in polynomial time.
Incidence-capacity lower bound: if rho=max_v |N[v]| and a solution has k bugs, then L(n,k)≤k rho, where L(n,k) is the minimum total cardinality of n distinct nonempty subsets of a k-element set.

## Object

The `maxflow` family of the Part-B bug bank: a reference implementation with
seeded, realistic (LLM-slip-style) mutants, ported bit-exactly to Lean 4 as the
trusted library `QEDBugBank` (plain `Nat`/`List` data, structural recursion
only, so the kernel itself evaluates every run).

- Reference: `maxflowEK` — Edmonds-Karp (shortest augmenting paths), a Lean port bit-exact to the Python reference.
- Observable: `flowObsEq`: flow value, per-edge flows, and the canonical min cut.
- Seeded mutants admitted by the Python bank:
- `mutant_1` — forgets to add reverse residual edges (no flow cancellation); its minimal kill needs the n = 6 trap
- `mutant_3` — off-by-one: skips the last augmenting path when its bottleneck equals 1
- `mutant_4` — min cut computed from reachability in the original graph instead of the residual graph
- Enumerated witness space: 531,441 capacitated digraphs on 4 vertices (s = 0, t = 3, capacities in {0,1,2}; `allFlowNets 4`), plus a handcrafted n = 6 flow-cancellation trap.

## What it kills

The illusion that these mutants are benign — i.e. the claim that no small input
distinguishes them from the reference. Each admitted (mutant, test) pair
carries a kernel-checked admission theorem
`adm_maxflow__<mutant>__<test>` on its minimal canonical killing input:

- `mutant_1` killed by `test_differential_handcrafted`
- `mutant_1` killed by `test_differential_random_dags`
- `mutant_3` killed by `test_differential_handcrafted`
- `mutant_3` killed by `test_differential_random_dags`
- `mutant_3` killed by `test_differential_random_digraphs`
- `mutant_3` killed by `test_metamorphic_capacity_scaling`
- `mutant_3` killed by `test_property_mincut_certificate`
- `mutant_4` killed by `test_property_mincut_certificate`

## Why it works

The admission combinator proves, on the witness `w`: the reference satisfies
the family spec on `w` AND the mutant differs from the reference on the
observable (or violates the spec) on `w`. Killing inputs were extracted by
exhaustive enumeration in canonical order (first kill wins) and re-verified by
direct execution of the Python originals; the Lean port was differentially
validated against Python over exhaustive input spaces with no discrepancy.

## Debugging uses

- The killing inputs are ready-made minimal regression tests for maxflow
  implementations; each is a few tokens of literal data in the theorem statement.
- The mutants encode realistic fault patterns (comparator slips, off-by-one
  termination, stale state); checking new code against these witnesses probes
  exactly those patterns.

## Remarks

- All admission theorems in this family are KERNEL_PASS (see
  `lean/qedbench/bug_bank/results/verdicts.csv`).
- Bounded correctness of the reference (`bc_maxflow__maxflowEK_n4`) and the two bounded-equivalence certificates (`be_maxflow__mutantFlow1_n4`, `be_maxflow__mutantFlow2_n4`) exceeded the kernel budget (heartbeat timeout after hours) and pass only via `native_decide` (ND_PASS — compiler-trusted, weaker than the kernel-checked admission certificates above).
- Instances live in `lean/qedbench/bug_bank/instances/`
  (`adm_maxflow__*.lean`); the trusted surface is
  `lean/qedbench/QEDBugBank.lean`.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Vertices V = {0,1,2,3}; host graph G = T1 ∪ T2 = {01, 02, 03, 12, 23} (i.e. K4 minus the edge {1,3}).

T1 = {01, 02, 03}  (star centered at 0) — a spanning tree.
T2 = {01, 12, 23}  (path 0-1-2-3) — a spanning tree.
T1\T2 = {02, 03};  T2\T1 = {12, 23}.

Take e = {0,3} ∈ T1\T2, exactly as the proof does. Adding e to T2 creates the unique cycle C = 0-1-2-3-0, i.e. C = {01, 12, 23, 03}. Take f = {1,2}: it lies on C and f ∈ T2\T1, so it satisfies every hypothesis the proof imposes on the "f chosen from the cycle C".

The proof's sentence: "Adding f to T1 creates a cycle, and e is in this cycle."
Recomputed: T1 + f = {01, 02, 03, 12}; its unique cycle is 0-1-2-0 = {01, 02, 12}. The claim says e = {0,3} ∈ cycle(T1+f); here cycle(T1+f) = {01,02,12} and e = {0,3} ∉ {01,02,12}. The claim fails.

Consequence for the conclusion the proof draws: T1' = (T1\{e}) ∪ {f} = {01, 02, 12}. That is 3 edges on 4 vertices (correct count for a spanning tree), but it has 2 connected components ({0,1,2} and the isolated vertex {3}) and contains the cycle {01,02,12}. So T1' is NOT a spanning tree — it is simultaneously disconnected and cyclic, exactly the failure mode the target claim describes.

(Contrast: the companion exchange the proof also uses is fine here — T2' = (T2\{f}) ∪ {e} = {01, 03, 23} IS a spanning tree. So the asymmetry is real: f ∈ C guarantees T2 - f + e is a tree, but says nothing about T1 - e + f.)

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **In Case 2 the proof asserts that, for the edges e in T1\T2 and f in T2\T1 selected earlier (f chosen from the cycle C created by adding e to T2), adding f to T1 creates a cycle that contains e, so that T1' = (T1\{e}) union {f} is a spanning tree. This is false in general: the unique cycle of T1 + f need not contain e, in which case (T1\{e}) union {f} is not a spanning tree (it can be disconnected and contain a cycle), so the Case 2 contradiction does not follow.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Adding f to T1 creates a cycle, and e is in this cycle.

Context of the original problem:

> Problem Statement
> Problem: Algorithms - 37
> Consider an instance (G, c) of the Minimum Spanning Tree problem, assuming that the
> graph G is connected. Suppose further that the weight function c is injective on the edge
> set, such that c(e) ̸= c(e′) for all distinct pairs of edges e, e′. Prove that this problem
> instance admits a unique optimum solution.
> 1

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The asserted statement is finite and purely combinatorial: for all spanning trees T1, T2 of a graph G, all e ∈ T1\T2, and all f ∈ C(T2,e) ∩ (T2\T1), the unique cycle of T1+f contains e (hence (T1\{e})∪{f} is a spanning tree). A single finite (T1, T2, e, f) refutes it.

Since C(T2,e) ⊆ T2 ∪ {e} and cycle(T1+f) ⊆ T1 ∪ {f}, no edge outside T1 ∪ T2 can ever affect any object in the statement; therefore any counterexample inside a larger host graph G restricts to one with G = T1 ∪ T2. It suffices to enumerate pairs of labeled trees on a common vertex set.

The script exhaustively enumerates, for n = 3,4,5,6, all labeled trees via all Prüfer sequences (n^(n-2) trees: 3, 16, 125, 1296), all ordered pairs (T1,T2) (1,696,242 pairs total), all e ∈ T1\T2, all admissible f ∈ C(T2,e) ∩ (T2\T1) — 11,053,914 admissible quadruples. Of these, 4,512,960 (40.83%) violate the claim; the lexicographically first witness occurs already at n = 4 and is reported above. All computation is exact integer/set combinatorics (BFS tree paths, component counts, explicit cycle extraction); no floats, no randomness, deterministic iteration order. Runtime ≈ 6.5 s CPU (about 2 min wall on the loaded node).

The script also tests the weaker "repair" reading — that at least one admissible f works for each (T1,T2,e). That reading held in all 5,636,610 admissible triples (0 failures), consistent with the symmetric exchange theorem for matroids/spanning trees. So the correct fix is that f must be selected as an edge of C whose removal from T1 ... more precisely f must be chosen to lie on the T1-fundamental cut of e (equivalently, e must lie on the T1-fundamental cycle of f), which needs a separate argument; the proof's blanket assertion that this holds for the already-chosen f is false, and the Case 2 contradiction does not follow as written.

Independent hand check of the witness: T1 = star {01,02,03}, T2 = path {01,12,23}, e = {0,3}, C = {01,12,23,03}, f = {1,2}; T1+f contains the triangle 0-1-2-0 which omits e; T1-e+f = {01,02,12} leaves vertex 3 isolated and contains a triangle.

## Remarks

- Provenance: record `Algorithms_37__sol3`, corpus "QEDBench, second-model flags (confirmed)" of the proof-verification canonical-600 confirmed set (commit e33026ae); full dossier in that repository's `iclr_submission/supplement_dossiers.pdf`.
- Verification: zero-import Lean 4 certificate vendored at `lean/canonical600/Algorithms_37__sol3.lean` (kernel-checked in the source pipeline; certificate route None).

## References

- Pipeline record: `qedbench_certificate_availability_triage/data/records_alg_graph.jsonl` (proof-verification repo, commit e33026ae).

## Object

Families of bipartite graphs H_r of degeneracy exactly r, together with
host-graph constructions witnessing ex(n; H_r) >= c n^(2 - 1/r + 1/(28 r^2)).
The exponent gap 1/(28 r^2) is small but polynomial — enough to refute the
conjectured exponent at every degeneracy level, not just at one.

## What it kills

The belief that degeneracy is the right parameter governing bipartite Turán
exponents — the organizing conjecture of degenerate extremal graph theory since
the 1960s. Decades of upper-bound results were read as progress toward it.

## Debugging uses

- Any argument that infers an upper bound ex(n; H) = O(n^(2-1/r)) from
  r-degeneracy alone is now simply wrong; the surviving hypotheses (bounded
  degree on one side) must be checked explicitly.
- The uniform-in-r refutation is a caution for "the conjecture is at least
  asymptotically right" fallbacks: the failure is not a boundary effect at
  small r.

## Remarks

Resolved together with the compactness conjecture (Erdős problem 180) in one
Lean file of OpenAI's ten-proofs collection; the second linked repository
extends the refutation to every degeneracy level with machine-checked
certificates.

## Object

The certificate witness, as recorded by the triage stage:

Counterexample to the VC⇒crossing direction: take K=1 and G as the star K_{1,3}, with center c and leaves x,y,z. Vertex cover {c} has size 1, so the VC instance is YES. The reduction sets k=2, so Charon can carry at most one passenger. The crossing instance is infeasible: the first trip must carry c, otherwise c is left with a leaf unsupervised. To move a leaf x, Charon can return alone and take x right. Then right has c and x; on returning, Charon must bring either c or x. Bringing x undoes progress; bringing c leaves c with y,z on the left. From there, carrying y or z would leave c with another leaf unsupervised, so the only safe move is carrying c back, returning to the same loop. A brute-force state search over 2*2^4 states verifies no goal state.

## What it kills

The flawed step of QEDBench problem Algorithms_11, solution 1, reads:

> We will show that for any graph G and any integer K ≥1, the following equivalence holds: G has a vertex cover of size ≤K ⇐⇒ the river crossing instance (G, k) with k := K + 1 is feasible.

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its
conclusion, refuting the step **as written** (not necessarily the problem's
headline theorem — see the module docstring for scope).

## Why it works

From the Lean module docstring
(`lean/qedbench/ProofCerts/Algorithms/Alg11.lean`):

**Algorithms_11 (sol1/2) — the VC ↔ river-crossing reduction equivalence fails**

Both candidate solutions reduce Vertex Cover to an Alcuin-style river-crossing puzzle:
the items to ferry are the vertices of a conflict graph `G`; the boat holds the ferryman
(Charon) plus at most `k − 1` items per crossing; a state is *safe* when the bank
**without** Charon contains no edge of `G` with both endpoints present; initially Charon
and all items are on the left bank, and the goal is everyone on the right bank. The
solutions assert the equivalences:

* **sol1**: "`G` has a vertex cover of size `≤ K` **iff** the river-crossing instance
  `(G, k = K + 1)` is feasible."
* **sol2**: "with exactly **one** crossing the instance is solvable **iff** `G` has a
  vertex cover of size `≤ k − 1`."

Both are **false** in the direction "vertex cover exists ⇒ the crossing succeeds".

**Counterexample to sol1 (`K = 1`, `G = K₁,₃`).** The star `K₁,₃` with center `c` and
leaves `x, y, z` (edges `c–x`, `c–y`, `c–z`) has the vertex cover `{c}` of size
`1 ≤ K = 1` (`vcC_covers`, `vcC_size_one`). The claimed equivalent crossing instance has
`k = K + 1 = 2`: Charon plus at most **one** item per crossing. That instance is
**infeasible** (the ferrying number of `K₁,₃` is `2`, not `1`): from the start Charon can
only ferry `c` (anything else strands `c` with a leaf), after which every continuation
shuttles among the nine states
`{0, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 16, 19}` — Charon can park `c` on the right, fetch one leaf, and
then must take `c` back before fetching the next leaf, undoing all progress. The
all-on-the-right state `31` is never reached. We certify unreachability in the `GT1`
closure-invariant style: the explicit `9`-state set `inReach` (given by the bitmask
`reachMask = 592285`) contains the start state (`start_in_reach`), is **closed** under
every legal-and-safe move (`reach_closed`), and excludes the goal (`goal_not_in_reach`).
Any feasible crossing schedule visits a `step`-path of states from `startState` to
`goalState`; a start-containing `step`-closed set traps every such path, so the goal
being outside `inReach` means **no schedule exists**. For emphasis, `safe_goal` shows
the goal state itself is safe (infeasibility is genuinely a reachability obstruction),
and `start_moves` shows ferrying `c` is the *only* legal first move.

**Counterexample to sol2 (`G = K₂`, `k = 2`).** `K₂` (vertices `v₀, v₁`, one edge) has
the vertex cover `{v₁}` of size `1 = k − 1` (`vcH_covers`, `vcH_size_one`). But ONE
crossing moves Charon plus at most `k − 1 = 1` item, so at least one of the two items
stays on the left bank: enumerating all `8` candidate post-crossing states, the legal
outcomes from the start are exactly `{1, 3, 5}` (carry nothing / carry `v₀` / carry
`v₁`) — never the goal state `7` (`one_crossing_outcomes`, `one_crossing_capacity`).
So "solvable with exactly one crossing" fails although a vertex cover of size `k − 1`
exists, refuting sol2's equivalence (its "if" direction).

**Modeling choices**

* **sol1 state space**: a state is `Fin 32`, read as five bits — bit `0` is Charon's
  side, bit `i + 1` is the side of item `i` (`0 = c`, `1 = x`, `2 = y`, `3 = z`);
  side `false`/`0` = left (start) bank, `true`/`1` = right (goal) bank. So
  `startState = 0` and `goalState = 31`. Bits are extracted with the kernel-accelerated
  operations `>>>`, `%`, `==` only.
* `edgesG` lists the three star edges; `safe s` says no edge has both endpoints on the
  Charon-less bank. A move `legalMove p s` requires: Charon switches banks; at most one
  item changes banks (`movedCount p s ≤ 1` via `Nat.ble`, i.e. boat capacity
  `k = 2` counting Charon); and any item that moves starts on Charon's old bank
  (`ridesWithCharon` — it rides the boat, hence lands on Charon's new bank).
  `step p s = legalMove p s && safe s` demands safety only of the **target** state;
  this is *more permissive* than the real puzzle (which also needs `safe p`), so our
  unreachability certificate is only **stronger**.
* `inReach` is membership in the bitmask `reachMask = 592285`, whose set bits
  `{0, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 16, 19}` are exactly the BFS closure of the start state under
  `step` (verified numerically). All facts are `decide`-checked over `Fin 32` pairs —
  no `Finset`, no function-type enumeration, no `native_decide`, in the style of `GT1`'s
  separator certificate (`A_closed`).
* **sol2 state space**: `Fin 8` (bit `0` Charon, bits `1`–`2` the two `K₂` vertices),
  `startH = 0`, `goalH = 7`, same move rules with capacity `k − 1 = 1`. The claim's
  "solvable with exactly one crossing" is the decidable proposition `Sol2Claim`:
  some state reachable in one legal safe crossing equals `goalH`; it is refuted in the
  `GT20` unpacking style (`sol2_claim_fails`).
* Vertex covers are `Bool`-valued membership functions; `coversG`/`coversH` check every
  listed edge has a covered endpoint, and sizes are explicit sums of `Bool.toNat`
  (no `Finset.card`), as in `GT1`'s `degree`.

## Debugging uses

- The witness is a minimal, machine-checked regression input for any proof or
  implementation that leans on this step; rebuilding the Lean module re-verifies it.
- The module states the claim faithfully in Mathlib vocabulary; its definitions
  can be reused to audit neighboring steps of the same proof.

Minimal witness (found first in an enumeration ordered by node count, edge count, then total weight; independently verified by hand):

Digraph on 3 nodes {s, a, b}, source s, arcs with positive integer weights:
  s->a (w=1),  s->b (w=3),  a->b (w=1)
Intra-iteration relaxation order (fixed, standard in-place Bellman-Ford): s->a, then s->b, then a->b.
k = 1 iteration; offending node u = b.

Trace of the in-place algorithm (exact integers, "inf" = uninitialised):
  after 0 iterations: dist = {s:0, a:inf, b:inf}
  iteration 1: relax s->a  => dist[a] = 0+1 = 1
               relax s->b  => dist[b] = 0+3 = 3
               relax a->b  => 1+1 = 2 < 3, so dist[b] = 2   (this relaxation sees the dist[a] just updated in the same iteration)
  after 1 iteration: dist = {s:0, a:1, b:2}

Reference quantity: the s-b paths with at most 1 edge are exactly {s->b}, of length 3. So OPT_1(b) = 3.

The hypothesis of the claim is satisfied (b does have an s-b path with at most k=1 edges), yet:
  CLAIM says dist[b] after 1 iteration EQUALS OPT_1(b) = 3;
  HERE      dist[b] = 2 < 3.
The equality invariant therefore fails. Note dist[b] = 2 is the length of a genuine s-b path (s->a->b), just one using 2 > k edges — exactly the failure mode of an in-place iteration propagating along several edges in a favourable processing order.

Aggregate over the whole exhausted space: 38,640 (instance, order, k, node) equality violations, every single one of them in the direction dist[u] < OPT_k(u); zero violations in the direction dist[u] > OPT_k(u).

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The stated Bellman-Ford loop invariant claims exact equality: after k iterations, for any node u reachable by a path of at most k edges, dist[u] EQUALS the minimum length of an s-u path with at most k edges. For the standard in-place Bellman-Ford (relaxations within an iteration see already-updated distances), this equality claim is false: dist[u] can be strictly smaller than the best <=k-edge path length, because a single iteration can propagate updates along several edges when they are processed in a favorable order. The correct invariant is an inequality (dist[u] <= min length over <=k-edge paths, and dist[u] is always the length of some s-u path). The induction step 3 tacitly assumes dist values are frozen during an iteration, which the actual algorithm does not guarantee.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> After k (k >= 0) iterations of relaxations, for any node **u** that has at least one path from **s** (the start node) to **u** with at most **k** edges, the distance of from **s** to **u** is the smallest length of a path from **s** to **u** that contains at most **k** edges.

Context of the original problem:

> Clarification in the proof for the Bellamn-Ford algorithm

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The verbatim sentence asserts an exact equality: after k iterations, for every node u having some s-u path with at most k edges, dist[u] = min length over s-u paths with at most k edges. This is a finitely refutable universally quantified statement over (digraph, weights, source, relaxation order, k, u), so a single finite instance refutes it.

The script formalises the standard textbook Bellman-Ford exactly as written (dist[s]=0, others infinite; n-1 iterations; within each iteration relax every arc once in a fixed order, IN PLACE so later relaxations see updates made earlier in the same iteration). The edge order is not specified by the algorithm, so every permutation is a legitimate instantiation and is searched. The reference value OPT_k(u) is computed independently by explicit enumeration of simple s-u paths with at most k edges, not by any dynamic program that could inherit the same bug. All weights are strictly positive, so "min over walks with <= k edges" and "min over simple paths with <= k edges" coincide — the walk/path reading of the claim cannot change the verdict. All arithmetic is Python int; infinity is a sentinel 10**6 that exceeds any achievable finite distance (<= 5 arcs x weight 4 = 20) and is never used as an arithmetic operand (relaxation is attempted only from a strictly finite dist). No floats, no randomness, no external libraries; the run is fully deterministic.

The search found a witness immediately and it reproduces by hand (see witness description): dist[b] = 2 after one iteration while the best <=1-edge s-b path has length 3.

Two controls corroborate the diagnosis rather than merely the failure:
(A) Over the entire exhausted space, the inequality dist_after_k[u] <= OPT_k(u) was NEVER violated (0 of 38,640 discrepancies were in the ">" direction), and every discrepancy had dist[u] equal to the length of some actual s-u path using more than k edges. So the corrected invariant proposed (an inequality, with dist always realised by some genuine path) is consistent with all the evidence, while the asserted equality is not.
(C) Negative control: the synchronous / "frozen" variant of the same loop (each iteration relaxes only from the previous iteration's snapshot) produced ZERO equality violations anywhere in the space. This pins the failure precisely on in-place updating, i.e. on the induction step's tacit assumption that dist values are frozen during an iteration.
(D) Honest caveat: no digraph in the space violated the equality under EVERY arc order — for each one, some order (roughly, a reverse-topological order) makes the equality hold. The witness is therefore order-dependent. That does not weaken the refutation: standard Bellman-Ford fixes no arc order, so the universally quantified invariant as stated is false; it only holds for specially chosen orders (or for the frozen-snapshot variant).

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Single-machine fixed-start-time scheduling instance with THREE equal-length jobs (so the length spread is k = max|j_i|/min|j_i| = 1), given as (start, length, profit):

  J1 = (0, 2, 2)  -> occupies [0,2)
  J2 = (1, 2, 3)  -> occupies [1,3)
  J3 = (2, 2, 2)  -> occupies [2,4)

Feasibility = pairwise non-overlapping half-open intervals. J2 conflicts with both J1 and J3; J1 and J3 are compatible ([0,2) and [2,4) only touch).

GREEDY (take the feasible job of biggest profit, repeatedly): first picks J2 (profit 3, the unique maximum), after which J1 and J3 are both infeasible. GREEDY = 3. This is greedy's BEST case over every tie-breaking rule (the script maximizes over all orderings consistent with non-increasing profit), so no tie-breaking convention rescues it.

OPT = {J1, J3} = 2 + 2 = 4.

Recomputed quantities: k = 1; claim requires GREEDY >= OPT/(k-eps), and a fortiori GREEDY >= OPT/k = 4/1 = 4; here GREEDY = 3 < 4. Ratio GREEDY/OPT = 3/4 < 1 = 1/k, and 1/(k-eps) = 1/(1-eps) > 1 > 3/4 for every eps in (0,1), so the asserted bound fails for every eps > 0 admissible.

(Scaling the profits, e.g. (0,2,n), (1,2,n+1), (2,2,n), drives the ratio to (n+1)/(2n) -> 1/2, so the true worst case for k = 1 is 1/2, not 1.)

  after 1 iteration: dist = {s:0, a:1, b:2}

The hypothesis of the claim is satisfied (b does have an s-b path with at most k=1 edges), yet:

  HERE      dist[b] = 2 < 3.
The equality invariant therefore fails. Note dist[b] = 2 is the length of a genuine s-b path (s->a->b), just one using 2 > k edges — exactly the failure mode of an in-place iteration propagating along several edges in a favourable processing order.

The flagged claim: **The stated Bellman-Ford loop invariant claims exact equality: after k iterations, for any node u reachable by a path of at most k edges, dist[u] EQUALS the minimum length of an s-u path with at most k edges. The correct invariant is an inequality (dist[u] <= min length over <=k-edge paths, and dist[u] is always the length of some s-u path). The induction step 3 tacitly assumes dist values are frozen during an iteration, which the actual algorithm does not guarantee.**

> After k (k >= 0) iterations of relaxations, for any node **u** that has at least one path from **s** (the start node) to **u** with at most **k** edges, the distance of from **s** to **u** is the smallest length of a path from **s** to **u** that contains at most **k** edges.

> Clarification in the proof for the Bellamn-Ford algorithm

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

The verbatim sentence asserts an exact equality: after k iterations, for every node u having some s-u path with at most k edges, dist[u] = min length over s-u paths with at most k edges. This is a finitely refutable universally quantified statement over (digraph, weights, source, relaxation order, k, u), so a single finite instance refutes it.

The script formalises the standard textbook Bellman-Ford exactly as written (dist[s]=0, others infinite; n-1 iterations; within each iteration relax every arc once in a fixed order, IN PLACE so later relaxations see updates made earlier in the same iteration). The edge order is not specified by the algorithm, so every permutation is a legitimate instantiation and is searched. ## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

A two-type family population, all rational, no gender-responsive stopping rule, both boy-probabilities strictly interior:

  Type A: n = 2 children, boy-probability p_A = 3/4, population weight 1/2
  Type B: n = 3 children, boy-probability p_B = 1/2, population weight 1/2

Family size is a static attribute fixed in advance (children i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) given the type), so there is NO "family planning" / stopping rule reacting to realized sexes. The boy-probability IS heterogeneous across families (3/4 vs 1/2), so the claim's hypothesis holds.

Recomputed quantities (exact Fractions; K = boys, N = family size):
  E[K(K-1)]   = 1/2·2·1·(3/4)^2 + 1/2·3·2·(1/2)^2       = 21/16
  E[K]        = 1/2·2·(3/4) + 1/2·3·(1/2)               = 3/2
  E[#brothers | uniformly random MAN]   = (21/16)/(3/2) = 7/8   = 0.875
  E[K(N-K)]   = 1/2·2·1·(3/4)(1/4) + 1/2·3·2·(1/2)(1/2) = 15/16
  E[N-K]      = 1/2·2·(1/4) + 1/2·3·(1/2)               = 1
  E[#brothers | uniformly random WOMAN] = (15/16)/1     = 15/16 = 0.9375

So MAN (14/16) < WOMAN (15/16), deficit exactly 1/16 — the opposite of the asserted "men on average have more brothers". Both averages were independently re-derived by brute-force enumeration of all 2^n sex sequences of each family type with exact rational sequence probabilities, counting brothers person-by-person; the enumeration agrees exactly with the closed form (assertion in the script).

Also reported by the script: a still simpler degenerate witness ({n=1,p=1,w=1/2} + {n=2,p=1/2,w=1/2}: men 1/4 vs women 1/2) and a largest-gap witness ({n=1,p=1,w=7/8} + {n=6,p=7/8,w=1/8}: men 15/8 vs women 35/8). 1890 of the 9072 enumerated heterogeneous mixtures reverse the claimed inequality.

Mechanism: within one family type both a boy and a girl expect (n-1)p brothers; the population averages are the SAME numbers (n_i-1)p_i reweighted, by n_i·p_i·w_i for men versus n_i·(1-p_i)·w_i for women. Heterogeneity in p only guarantees the male tilt is toward high-p families; it gives men more brothers only if (n-1)p is increasing in p, which requires size to be uncorrelated with propensity. In the witness the low-p families are the LARGER ones, so (n-1)p is decreasing in p (3/4 for the p=3/4 type, 1 for the p=1/2 type) and the male size-bias points at the families with fewer brothers.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The answer's "in real life" conclusion (also its headline claim on line 0004) that heterogeneity of the boy-probability across families implies men have more brothers: "If the likelihood of having boys does depend on the family, men on average have more brothers, not fewer." This is asserted as a general implication of family-level heterogeneity in p, with only gender-responsive "family planning" excluded. It is false whenever family size is (statically) correlated with the family's boy-propensity, which heterogeneity alone does not preclude.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> If the likelihood of having boys does depend on the family, men on average have more brothers, not fewer.

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Do men or women have more brothers?
> 
> Do men or women have more brothers?
> 
> I think women have more as no man can be his own brother. But how one can prove it rigorously?
> 
> I am going to suggest some reasonable background assumptions:
> 
> There are a large number of individuals, of whom half are men and half are women.
> The individuals are partitioned into nonempty families.
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The verbatim sentence asserts a general implication: heterogeneity of the per-family boy-probability (with gender-responsive family planning explicitly excluded) implies E[#brothers | random man] > E[#brothers | random woman]. This is a finitely refutable statement — a witness is a finite family-type mixture with rational sizes, propensities and weights, and both conditional expectations are then rational and exactly computable as E[K(K-1)]/E[K] and E[K(N-K)]/E[N-K].

The claim is false as stated. Heterogeneity in p alone is not enough; one also needs family SIZE to be uninformative about the family's boy-propensity. The witness above satisfies every stated hypothesis (heterogeneous p, static family sizes, no stopping rule reacting to realized sexes) yet yields men 7/8 < women 15/16 brothers. Nothing in the claim's stated hypotheses precludes a static correlation between family size and boy-propensity, and such a correlation is not "family planning" in the sense the answer excludes — the number of children is fixed in advance and never reacts to which sexes actually appear.

Two exhaustive controls in the script confirm the diagnosis rather than a modelling slip:
  (C1) Homogeneous baseline: for all 42 single-type populations with 0<p<1 and n in 1..6, B_men == B_women EXACTLY, reproducing the classical "no difference" result the answer is arguing against.
  (C2) Equal-size control: over all 1512 two-type mixtures with n1 == n2 (size carries no information about p), there were ZERO violations of B_men >= B_women. So the answer's conclusion IS correct under the unstated extra hypothesis "family size uncorrelated with boy-propensity", and the flagged gap is precisely the omission of that hypothesis.
  (C3) Every reported witness's two averages were recomputed by direct person-by-person enumeration of all sex sequences and matched the closed form exactly (asserted, not merely printed).

All arithmetic is fractions.Fraction/int; no float is created anywhere and no decision is made from a float (decimals are printed only via an exact Fraction-to-string helper). The script is deterministic, stdlib-only, and runs in about 0.5 s.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

The written step "rho(X u {y}) <= rho(X) + rho({y}) - rho(X u {y})", equivalently 2*rho(X u {y}) <= rho(X) + rho({y}), fails on genuine matroid rank functions. Two verified witnesses printed by the script:

(1) SMALLEST: ground set S = {e1}, the free matroid U_{1,1} (independent sets: {}, {e1}), so rho({}) = 0, rho({e1}) = 1. Take X = {} (empty) and y = e1, so y not in X. Then rho(X) = 0, rho({y}) = 1, rho(X u {y}) = 1, rho(X n {y}) = rho({}) = 0. The written inequality reads 1 <= 0 + 1 - 1 = 0, which is FALSE since 1 > 0. Equivalently 2*rho(X u {y}) = 2 > rho(X) + rho({y}) = 1.

(2) NON-DEGENERATE (X nonempty): ground set S = {e1, e2}, matroid with independent sets {}, {e1} (e2 is a loop): rho({}) = 0, rho({e1}) = 1, rho({e2}) = 0, rho({e1,e2}) = 1. Take X = {e1}, y = e2 (y not in X). Then rho(X) = 1, rho({y}) = 0, rho(X u {y}) = 1, rho(X n {y}) = 0. Written step: 1 <= 1 + 0 - 1 = 0, FALSE since 1 > 0; equivalently 2*1 = 2 > 1 + 0 = 1.

Both rho are actual matroid rank functions, obtained as rho(A) = max{|I| : I independent, I subseteq A} from an enumerated independence system, and the script explicitly re-verifies EVERY rank-axiom variant on them so that the witness cannot be dismissed on a question of which numbering (R4)-(R6) denotes: (R1) 0 <= rho(A) <= |A|; (R2) monotonicity; (R3) submodularity rho(A u B) + rho(A n B) <= rho(A) + rho(B); (R4) rho(empty) = 0; (R5) unit increase rho(A) <= rho(A u {x}) <= rho(A) + 1; (R6a) the local closure axiom rho(A u {x}) = rho(A u {z}) = rho(A) => rho(A u {x,z}) = rho(A); and (R6b) the CORRECTED one-element submodularity rho(A u {y}) <= rho(A) + rho({y}) - rho(A n {y}). All print "holds".

The corrected step is satisfied on the witnesses (e.g. witness 2: rho(X u {y}) = 1 <= rho(X) + rho({y}) - rho(X n {y}) = 1 + 0 - 0 = 1), confirming that the discrepancy is exactly the subtracted term: rho(X n {y}) (= 0 when y not in X) was mistyped as rho(X u {y}).

Violations are pervasive, not exotic: 87 of the 91 matroid rank functions on ground sets of size <= 4 admit a pair (X, y) with y not in X violating the written inequality. In fact the step fails for EVERY (X, y) with y not in X and rho(X u {y}) > rho(X) + rho({y}) - rho(X n {y}) + ... more simply, whenever rho(X u {y}) > 0 and rho(X) + rho({y}) < 2*rho(X u {y}), which includes the free matroid U_{2,2} with X = {a}, y = b (2*2 = 4 > 1 + 1 = 2).

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **In the (R2) derivation the proof asserts, citing rank axiom (R6), that rho(X union {y}) <= rho(X) + rho({y}) - rho(X union {y}); the subtracted term should be rho(X intersect {y}). The written inequality (equivalently 2*rho(X union {y}) <= rho(X) + rho({y})) is false for legitimate rank functions satisfying R4-R6, so the cited step does not follow from R6.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> | r = \map \rho X + \map \rho {\set y} - \map \rho {X \cup \set y}

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Equivalence of Definitions of Matroid Rank Axioms/Formulation 2 Implies Formulation 1
> 
> Let $S$ be a finite set.
> 
> Let $\rho : \powerset S \to \Z$ be a mapping from the power set of $S$ to the integers.
> 
> Let $\rho$ satisfy formulation 2 of the rank axioms:
> {{begin-axiom}}
> {{axiom | n = \text R 4
>         | q = \forall X \in \powerset S
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The target claim asserts that the proof's written inequality does not follow from the cited rank axiom, because the inequality 2*rho(X u {y}) <= rho(X) + rho({y}) is false for legitimate rank functions. This is a universally quantified statement over rank functions and pairs (X, y), so a single finite rank function with one violating pair refutes the proof step outright; the claim of error is therefore finitely witnessable, and a witness was found.

Method (deterministic, stdlib-only, exact integer arithmetic; no floats anywhere; all quantities are set cardinalities and ranks compared with integer <, <=, ==):

(A) Matroid enumeration. For n = 1, 2, 3, 4 the script enumerates EVERY family I subseteq 2^[n] (all 2^(2^n) families; 65536 for n = 4) and keeps exactly the matroid independence systems, checking (I1) empty set in I, (I2) downward closure, (I3) the augmentation/exchange property. Rank is then computed as rho(A) = max{|I| : I in I, I subseteq A}. This yields all matroids on labeled ground sets of size <= 4. Independent validation of the enumerator: it produces 2, 5, 16, 68 rank functions for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, which matches the known counts of matroids on n labeled elements (1, 2, 5, 16, 68, 406, ...). Each enumerated rho is then asserted to satisfy all seven axiom checks (R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6a, R6b) — the assertion never fires, confirming these are legitimate rank functions under every axiom-set reading. For each rho, all (X, y) with X subseteq [n] and y in [n]\X are tested against 2*rho(X u {y}) <= rho(X) + rho({y}): 4780 (X, y) pairs tested in total.

(B) Raw function enumeration (robustness against a different meaning of "R4-R6"). Independently, for n = 1, 2, 3 the script enumerates EVERY function rho : 2^[n] -> {0,...,n} (4^8 = 65536 functions for n = 3) and keeps those satisfying only the weak local axiom set (R4) rho(empty) = 0, (R5) unit increase, (R6a) the local closure axiom — no submodularity or matroid structure assumed. It finds 2, 5, 16 such functions for n = 1, 2, 3 (all of which coincide with the matroid rank functions, itself a confirmation of the standard equivalence-of-axioms theorem), of which 1, 4, 15 respectively violate the written inequality. So the counterexamples are not an artifact of imposing full matroid structure: they already exist under the weakest reading of "satisfies R4-R6".

Result: counterexamples exist and are ubiquitous (87 of 91 matroids on n <= 4). The written step is not merely unjustified by the cited axiom; it is a false inequality about rank functions in general. The corrected form with rho(X n {y}) subtracted holds on every enumerated rho (check R6b passes universally), which pins the defect precisely to the subtracted term. Runtime: 0.10 s, well inside the 3-minute budget. No web access or external material was consulted; the witness was constructed solely from the claim text.

Verification notes from the pipeline:

> Both finite witnesses satisfy all stated rank-axiom variants and falsify the written inequality. Incidental enumeration totals in the input are inaccurate: 65,812 candidate families were examined (not 65,810), and 2,390 pairs were tested (not 4,780); this does not affect the counterexample.
> Hypotheses independently checked: Matroid independence axioms I1-I3; Rank axioms R1-R6a and corrected R6b; Smallest U_{1,1} witness; Nondegenerate loop witness; Exhaustive n=1..4 matroid enumeration; Corrected-inequality negative control
> Claimed result: The written inequality follows from the cited rank axiom for legitimate rank functions.
> Actual result: False: valid witnesses make the written inequality read 1 <= 0; 87 of 91 enumerated rank functions admit a violation.
> Negative control: The nearby corrected inequality, subtracting rho(X intersect {y}), holds for the nondegenerate witness.
> Verifier correction: rho(X union {y}) <= rho(X)+rho({y})-rho(X intersect {y}); for X={e1}, y=e2, this is 1 <= 1.
> The independent Terra checker exited 0 and its stdout was rerun and byte-matched by the collection harness.

The certificate witness, as recorded by the triage stage:

Take H to be a 6-cycle v0-v1-v2-v3-v4-v5-v0 with alternating colors: v0,v2,v4 red and v1,v3,v5 blue. Add the ear/chord P=v0v3 of length 1, drawn inside the hexagon. P has odd length, but its endpoints are red and blue, so adding it creates no monochromatic edge. The resulting plane graph has face lengths 6,4,4, all even.

## What it kills

The flawed step of QEDBench problem Graph Theory_12, solution 5, reads:

> If the length of P is odd, the other endpoint would receive the same color as the starting point, leading to a monochromatic edge when P is added.

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its
conclusion, refuting the step **as written** (not necessarily the problem's
headline theorem — see the module docstring for scope).

## Why it works

From the Lean module docstring
(`lean/qedbench/ProofCerts/GraphTheory/GT12.lean`):

**Graph Theory_12 (sol5) — an odd-length ear need NOT create a monochromatic edge**

The candidate solution claims:

> "If the ear/path `P` has ODD length, its far endpoint receives the SAME color as the
>  start, creating a monochromatic edge when `P` is added."

This is **false**. In a proper 2-coloring of a cycle the colors alternate, so along *any*
path the parity argument only forces "same color ⇔ even length" *when the path's internal
vertices are constrained to lie on that one alternating walk*. An ear is a brand-new path:
its far endpoint already has whatever color the existing graph assigned it, independently
of the ear's length. So an odd-length ear can perfectly well join two **differently**
colored vertices, in which case the new edge is bichromatic and creates no monochromatic
edge at all.

**Concrete witness.** The 6-cycle `v0–v1–v2–v3–v4–v5–v0` properly 2-colored alternately:

* `v0, v2, v4` are RED  (`color = true`);
* `v1, v3, v5` are BLUE (`color = false`).

This is a proper 2-coloring: every cycle edge joins a red to a blue vertex.

Now add the chord/ear `P = v0v3`, a single edge — so `P` has length `1`, which is **ODD**.
The endpoints are `v0` (RED) and `v3` (BLUE): they have **different** colors. Hence adding
the edge `v0v3` creates **no** monochromatic edge, directly refuting the claim that an
odd-length ear forces the far endpoint to match the start color.

(The arithmetic behind the failure: on a 6-cycle, `v0` and `v3` are at cycle-distance `3`,
an odd number of steps, so along the *cycle* their colors differ. The claim conflates the
*ear's* length with the *cycle distance* between the endpoints; here the ear has length `1`
while the endpoints sit at an odd cycle distance, so they are oppositely colored.)

**Modeling choices**
* Vertices are `Fin 6`, with `vi := i`. The undirected, loop-free 6-cycle is the explicit
  symmetric `Bool` adjacency `cycleAdj`, built from its six edges (style of `GT7`/`GT1`).
* The proper 2-coloring is `color : Fin 6 → Bool`, `true = red`, `false = blue`, with
  `color i = (i % 2 == 0)` so `v0,v2,v4 ↦ red` and `v1,v3,v5 ↦ blue`.
* "Properly 2-colored" is the decidable statement that every cycle edge is bichromatic:
  `∀ x y, cycleAdj x y = true → color x ≠ color y`, quantified over `Fin 6` and closed
  by `decide` (no `Finset` cardinalities, no enumeration of function types).
* The ear `P = v0v3` is a single edge `earAdj`; its length is the explicit `Nat`
  `earLength = 1`. `earLength % 2 = 1` certifies "odd length".
* "Monochromatic edge created by adding `P`" means the new edge's endpoints share a color,
  i.e. `color 0 = color 3`. We prove `color 0 ≠ color 3`, so the added edge is bichromatic.
  Every theorem is `by decide` over `Fin 6` / `Bool` / `Nat` (or a term built from such).

Reading the claim as an implication — "the ear is odd ⇒ its endpoints share a color" — the
witness makes the hypothesis TRUE (`ear_odd_length`) and the conclusion FALSE
(`ear_endpoints_differ`). We package this both as the negated conjunction `claim_fails`
(GT20 style) and as the directly-negated implication `claim_implication_fails`.

## Object

Minimal witness (found first in an enumeration ordered by node count, edge count, then total weight; independently verified by hand):

Digraph on 3 nodes {s, a, b}, source s, arcs with positive integer weights:
  s->a (w=1),  s->b (w=3),  a->b (w=1)
Intra-iteration relaxation order (fixed, standard in-place Bellman-Ford): s->a, then s->b, then a->b.
k = 1 iteration; offending node u = b.

Trace of the in-place algorithm (exact integers, "inf" = uninitialised):
  after 0 iterations: dist = {s:0, a:inf, b:inf}
  iteration 1: relax s->a  => dist[a] = 0+1 = 1
               relax s->b  => dist[b] = 0+3 = 3
               relax a->b  => 1+1 = 2 < 3, so dist[b] = 2   (this relaxation sees the dist[a] just updated in the same iteration)
  after 1 iteration: dist = {s:0, a:1, b:2}

Reference quantity: the s-b paths with at most 1 edge are exactly {s->b}, of length 3. So OPT_1(b) = 3.

The hypothesis of the claim is satisfied (b does have an s-b path with at most k=1 edges), yet:
  CLAIM says dist[b] after 1 iteration EQUALS OPT_1(b) = 3;
  HERE      dist[b] = 2 < 3.
The equality invariant therefore fails. Note dist[b] = 2 is the length of a genuine s-b path (s->a->b), just one using 2 > k edges — exactly the failure mode of an in-place iteration propagating along several edges in a favourable processing order.

Aggregate over the whole exhausted space: 38,640 (instance, order, k, node) equality violations, every single one of them in the direction dist[u] < OPT_k(u); zero violations in the direction dist[u] > OPT_k(u).

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The stated Bellman-Ford loop invariant claims exact equality: after k iterations, for any node u reachable by a path of at most k edges, dist[u] EQUALS the minimum length of an s-u path with at most k edges. For the standard in-place Bellman-Ford (relaxations within an iteration see already-updated distances), this equality claim is false: dist[u] can be strictly smaller than the best <=k-edge path length, because a single iteration can propagate updates along several edges when they are processed in a favorable order. The correct invariant is an inequality (dist[u] <= min length over <=k-edge paths, and dist[u] is always the length of some s-u path). The induction step 3 tacitly assumes dist values are frozen during an iteration, which the actual algorithm does not guarantee.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> After k (k >= 0) iterations of relaxations, for any node **u** that has at least one path from **s** (the start node) to **u** with at most **k** edges, the distance of from **s** to **u** is the smallest length of a path from **s** to **u** that contains at most **k** edges.

Context of the original problem:

> Clarification in the proof for the Bellamn-Ford algorithm

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The verbatim sentence asserts an exact equality: after k iterations, for every node u having some s-u path with at most k edges, dist[u] = min length over s-u paths with at most k edges. This is a finitely refutable universally quantified statement over (digraph, weights, source, relaxation order, k, u), so a single finite instance refutes it.

The script formalises the standard textbook Bellman-Ford exactly as written (dist[s]=0, others infinite; n-1 iterations; within each iteration relax every arc once in a fixed order, IN PLACE so later relaxations see updates made earlier in the same iteration). The edge order is not specified by the algorithm, so every permutation is a legitimate instantiation and is searched. The reference value OPT_k(u) is computed independently by explicit enumeration of simple s-u paths with at most k edges, not by any dynamic program that could inherit the same bug. All weights are strictly positive, so "min over walks with <= k edges" and "min over simple paths with <= k edges" coincide — the walk/path reading of the claim cannot change the verdict. All arithmetic is Python int; infinity is a sentinel 10**6 that exceeds any achievable finite distance (<= 5 arcs x weight 4 = 20) and is never used as an arithmetic operand (relaxation is attempted only from a strictly finite dist). No floats, no randomness, no external libraries; the run is fully deterministic.

The search found a witness immediately and it reproduces by hand (see witness description): dist[b] = 2 after one iteration while the best <=1-edge s-b path has length 3.

Two controls corroborate the diagnosis rather than merely the failure:
(A) Over the entire exhausted space, the inequality dist_after_k[u] <= OPT_k(u) was NEVER violated (0 of 38,640 discrepancies were in the ">" direction), and every discrepancy had dist[u] equal to the length of some actual s-u path using more than k edges. So the corrected invariant proposed (an inequality, with dist always realised by some genuine path) is consistent with all the evidence, while the asserted equality is not.
(C) Negative control: the synchronous / "frozen" variant of the same loop (each iteration relaxes only from the previous iteration's snapshot) produced ZERO equality violations anywhere in the space. This pins the failure precisely on in-place updating, i.e. on the induction step's tacit assumption that dist values are frozen during an iteration.
(D) Honest caveat: no digraph in the space violated the equality under EVERY arc order — for each one, some order (roughly, a reverse-topological order) makes the equality hold. The witness is therefore order-dependent. That does not weaken the refutation: standard Bellman-Ford fixes no arc order, so the universally quantified invariant as stated is false; it only holds for specially chosen orders (or for the frozen-snapshot variant).

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Minimal witness (found first in an enumeration ordered by node count, edge count, then total weight; independently verified by hand):

Digraph on 3 nodes {s, a, b}, source s, arcs with positive integer weights:
  s->a (w=1),  s->b (w=3),  a->b (w=1)
Intra-iteration relaxation order (fixed, standard in-place Bellman-Ford): s->a, then s->b, then a->b.
k = 1 iteration; offending node u = b.

Trace of the in-place algorithm (exact integers, "inf" = uninitialised):
  after 0 iterations: dist = {s:0, a:inf, b:inf}
  iteration 1: relax s->a  => dist[a] = 0+1 = 1
               relax s->b  => dist[b] = 0+3 = 3
               relax a->b  => 1+1 = 2 < 3, so dist[b] = 2   (this relaxation sees the dist[a] just updated in the same iteration)
  after 1 iteration: dist = {s:0, a:1, b:2}

Reference quantity: the s-b paths with at most 1 edge are exactly {s->b}, of length 3. So OPT_1(b) = 3.

The hypothesis of the claim is satisfied (b does have an s-b path with at most k=1 edges), yet:
  CLAIM says dist[b] after 1 iteration EQUALS OPT_1(b) = 3;
  HERE      dist[b] = 2 < 3.
The equality invariant therefore fails. Note dist[b] = 2 is the length of a genuine s-b path (s->a->b), just one using 2 > k edges — exactly the failure mode of an in-place iteration propagating along several edges in a favourable processing order.

Aggregate over the whole exhausted space: 38,640 (instance, order, k, node) equality violations, every single one of them in the direction dist[u] < OPT_k(u); zero violations in the direction dist[u] > OPT_k(u).

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The stated Bellman-Ford loop invariant claims exact equality: after k iterations, for any node u reachable by a path of at most k edges, dist[u] EQUALS the minimum length of an s-u path with at most k edges. For the standard in-place Bellman-Ford (relaxations within an iteration see already-updated distances), this equality claim is false: dist[u] can be strictly smaller than the best <=k-edge path length, because a single iteration can propagate updates along several edges when they are processed in a favorable order. The correct invariant is an inequality (dist[u] <= min length over <=k-edge paths, and dist[u] is always the length of some s-u path). The induction step 3 tacitly assumes dist values are frozen during an iteration, which the actual algorithm does not guarantee.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> After k (k >= 0) iterations of relaxations, for any node **u** that has at least one path from **s** (the start node) to **u** with at most **k** edges, the distance of from **s** to **u** is the smallest length of a path from **s** to **u** that contains at most **k** edges.

Context of the original problem:

> Clarification in the proof for the Bellamn-Ford algorithm

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The verbatim sentence asserts an exact equality: after k iterations, for every node u having some s-u path with at most k edges, dist[u] = min length over s-u paths with at most k edges. This is a finitely refutable universally quantified statement over (digraph, weights, source, relaxation order, k, u), so a single finite instance refutes it.

The script formalises the standard textbook Bellman-Ford exactly as written (dist[s]=0, others infinite; n-1 iterations; within each iteration relax every arc once in a fixed order, IN PLACE so later relaxations see updates made earlier in the same iteration). The edge order is not specified by the algorithm, so every permutation is a legitimate instantiation and is searched. The reference value OPT_k(u) is computed independently by explicit enumeration of simple s-u paths with at most k edges, not by any dynamic program that could inherit the same bug. All weights are strictly positive, so "min over walks with <= k edges" and "min over simple paths with <= k edges" coincide — the walk/path reading of the claim cannot change the verdict. All arithmetic is Python int; infinity is a sentinel 10**6 that exceeds any achievable finite distance (<= 5 arcs x weight 4 = 20) and is never used as an arithmetic operand (relaxation is attempted only from a strictly finite dist). No floats, no randomness, no external libraries; the run is fully deterministic.

The search found a witness immediately and it reproduces by hand (see witness description): dist[b] = 2 after one iteration while the best <=1-edge s-b path has length 3.

Two controls corroborate the diagnosis rather than merely the failure:
(A) Over the entire exhausted space, the inequality dist_after_k[u] <= OPT_k(u) was NEVER violated (0 of 38,640 discrepancies were in the ">" direction), and every discrepancy had dist[u] equal to the length of some actual s-u path using more than k edges. So the corrected invariant proposed (an inequality, with dist always realised by some genuine path) is consistent with all the evidence, while the asserted equality is not.
(C) Negative control: the synchronous / "frozen" variant of the same loop (each iteration relaxes only from the previous iteration's snapshot) produced ZERO equality violations anywhere in the space. This pins the failure precisely on in-place updating, i.e. on the induction step's tacit assumption that dist values are frozen during an iteration.
(D) Honest caveat: no digraph in the space violated the equality under EVERY arc order — for each one, some order (roughly, a reverse-topological order) makes the equality hold. The witness is therefore order-dependent. That does not weaken the refutation: standard Bellman-Ford fixes no arc order, so the universally quantified invariant as stated is false; it only holds for specially chosen orders (or for the frozen-snapshot variant).

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Single-machine fixed-start-time scheduling instance with THREE equal-length jobs (so the length spread is k = max|j_i|/min|j_i| = 1), given as (start, length, profit):

  J1 = (0, 2, 2)  -> occupies [0,2)
  J2 = (1, 2, 3)  -> occupies [1,3)
  J3 = (2, 2, 2)  -> occupies [2,4)

Feasibility = pairwise non-overlapping half-open intervals. J2 conflicts with both J1 and J3; J1 and J3 are compatible ([0,2) and [2,4) only touch).

GREEDY (take the feasible job of biggest profit, repeatedly): first picks J2 (profit 3, the unique maximum), after which J1 and J3 are both infeasible. GREEDY = 3. This is greedy's BEST case over every tie-breaking rule (the script maximizes over all orderings consistent with non-increasing profit), so no tie-breaking convention rescues it.

OPT = {J1, J3} = 2 + 2 = 4.

Recomputed quantities: k = 1; claim requires GREEDY >= OPT/(k-eps), and a fortiori GREEDY >= OPT/k = 4/1 = 4; here GREEDY = 3 < 4. Ratio GREEDY/OPT = 3/4 < 1 = 1/k, and 1/(k-eps) = 1/(1-eps) > 1 > 3/4 for every eps in (0,1), so the asserted bound fails for every eps > 0 admissible.

(Scaling the profits, e.g. (0,2,n), (1,2,n+1), (2,2,n), drives the ratio to (n+1)/(2n) -> 1/2, so the true worst case for k = 1 is 1/2, not 1.)

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The greedy algorithm (take the feasible job of biggest profit) on this fixed-start-time job-scheduling problem, where job lengths differ by at most a factor k (max_i |j_i| <= k * min_i |j_i|), achieves approximation factor 1/(k-epsilon) for any epsilon > 0; in particular for k = 1 (all lengths equal) this asserts greedy is (near-)optimal.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> So I figured since the problem is a k-Matroid (is this a common term?) there will be a an approximation factor $\frac{1}{k-\epsilon}$ for  any $\epsilon > 0.$

Context of the original problem:

> Single machine job scheduling (Greedy heuristic)

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The claim asserts that because the feasible sets form a "k-matroid" (k = length spread), greedy attains approximation factor 1/(k-eps) for every eps > 0; in particular for k = 1 (all lengths equal) greedy would be optimal. The weakest sensible formalization tested is GREEDY/OPT >= 1/k for every instance (weaker than 1/(k-eps), since 1/(k-eps) > 1/k for 0 < eps < k), so any violation refutes the claim a fortiori. For k = 1 the tested inequality is exactly "greedy is optimal".

The exhaustive search found 1221 violating instances out of 542,945 examined. The minimal witness is the 3-interval "blocking middle job" instance: equal lengths (k = 1), greedy = 3, OPT = 4, ratio 3/4 < 1. Structurally, the interval-scheduling independence system is not a matroid even with equal lengths (exchange fails: {J2} and {J1,J3} are both maximal independent but J2 cannot be extended), which is precisely why the "k-matroid => 1/(k-eps)" reasoning breaks. Greedy on this system is at best a 1/2-approximation for k = 1, and the correct general guarantee degrades further with k -- it is never the near-optimality the sentence claims.

Reliability: single machine, half-open intervals (touching allowed) is the standard reading of "fixed start time" job scheduling. Greedy was evaluated in its best case over all tie-breaks, and OPT by full subset enumeration; all arithmetic is exact (int / fractions.Fraction), no floats in any decision. Even under a multi-machine reading, the same instance with a single machine remains a legitimate instance of the problem class, and under any reading in which the middle job blocks the other two the counterexample stands.

## Object

Families of bipartite graphs H_r of degeneracy exactly r, together with
host-graph constructions witnessing ex(n; H_r) >= c n^(2 - 1/r + 1/(28 r^2)).
The exponent gap 1/(28 r^2) is small but polynomial — enough to refute the
conjectured exponent at every degeneracy level, not just at one.

## What it kills

The belief that degeneracy is the right parameter governing bipartite Turán
exponents — the organizing conjecture of degenerate extremal graph theory since
the 1960s. Decades of upper-bound results were read as progress toward it.

## Debugging uses

- Any argument that infers an upper bound ex(n; H) = O(n^(2-1/r)) from
  r-degeneracy alone is now simply wrong; the surviving hypotheses (bounded
  degree on one side) must be checked explicitly.
- The uniform-in-r refutation is a caution for "the conjecture is at least
  asymptotically right" fallbacks: the failure is not a boundary effect at
  small r.

## Remarks

Resolved together with the compactness conjecture (Erdős problem 180) in one
Lean file of OpenAI's ten-proofs collection; the second linked repository
extends the refutation to every degeneracy level with machine-checked
certificates.

> Title: Optimizing response times of an ambulance corp: short-term versus average

The symmetric antipodal configuration {0,1} analyzed in the post therefore correctly shows gap 0 (greedy = optimal = 3/4), confirming the post's own two-ambulance computation while showing its generalization fails.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Single-machine fixed-start-time scheduling instance with THREE equal-length jobs (so the length spread is k = max|j_i|/min|j_i| = 1), given as (start, length, profit):

  J1 = (0, 2, 2)  -> occupies [0,2)
  J2 = (1, 2, 3)  -> occupies [1,3)
  J3 = (2, 2, 2)  -> occupies [2,4)

Feasibility = pairwise non-overlapping half-open intervals. J2 conflicts with both J1 and J3; J1 and J3 are compatible ([0,2) and [2,4) only touch).

GREEDY (take the feasible job of biggest profit, repeatedly): first picks J2 (profit 3, the unique maximum), after which J1 and J3 are both infeasible. GREEDY = 3. This is greedy's BEST case over every tie-breaking rule (the script maximizes over all orderings consistent with non-increasing profit), so no tie-breaking convention rescues it.

OPT = {J1, J3} = 2 + 2 = 4.

Recomputed quantities: k = 1; claim requires GREEDY >= OPT/(k-eps), and a fortiori GREEDY >= OPT/k = 4/1 = 4; here GREEDY = 3 < 4. Ratio GREEDY/OPT = 3/4 < 1 = 1/k, and 1/(k-eps) = 1/(1-eps) > 1 > 3/4 for every eps in (0,1), so the asserted bound fails for every eps > 0 admissible.

(Scaling the profits, e.g. (0,2,n), (1,2,n+1), (2,2,n), drives the ratio to (n+1)/(2n) -> 1/2, so the true worst case for k = 1 is 1/2, not 1.)

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The greedy algorithm (take the feasible job of biggest profit) on this fixed-start-time job-scheduling problem, where job lengths differ by at most a factor k (max_i |j_i| <= k * min_i |j_i|), achieves approximation factor 1/(k-epsilon) for any epsilon > 0; in particular for k = 1 (all lengths equal) this asserts greedy is (near-)optimal.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> So I figured since the problem is a k-Matroid (is this a common term?) there will be a an approximation factor $\frac{1}{k-\epsilon}$ for  any $\epsilon > 0.$

Context of the original problem:

> Single machine job scheduling (Greedy heuristic)

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The claim asserts that because the feasible sets form a "k-matroid" (k = length spread), greedy attains approximation factor 1/(k-eps) for every eps > 0; in particular for k = 1 (all lengths equal) greedy would be optimal. The weakest sensible formalization tested is GREEDY/OPT >= 1/k for every instance (weaker than 1/(k-eps), since 1/(k-eps) > 1/k for 0 < eps < k), so any violation refutes the claim a fortiori. For k = 1 the tested inequality is exactly "greedy is optimal".

The exhaustive search found 1221 violating instances out of 542,945 examined. The minimal witness is the 3-interval "blocking middle job" instance: equal lengths (k = 1), greedy = 3, OPT = 4, ratio 3/4 < 1. Structurally, the interval-scheduling independence system is not a matroid even with equal lengths (exchange fails: {J2} and {J1,J3} are both maximal independent but J2 cannot be extended), which is precisely why the "k-matroid => 1/(k-eps)" reasoning breaks. Greedy on this system is at best a 1/2-approximation for k = 1, and the correct general guarantee degrades further with k -- it is never the near-optimality the sentence claims.

Reliability: single machine, half-open intervals (touching allowed) is the standard reading of "fixed start time" job scheduling. Greedy was evaluated in its best case over all tie-breaks, and OPT by full subset enumeration; all arithmetic is exact (int / fractions.Fraction), no floats in any decision. Even under a multi-machine reading, the same instance with a single machine remains a legitimate instance of the problem class, and under any reading in which the middle job blocks the other two the counterexample stands.
